{{Short description|String that certifies the answer to a computation}}
In [[computational complexity theory]], a '''certificate''' (also called a '''witness''') is a [[String (computer science)|string]] that certifies the answer to a [[computation]], or certifies the membership of some string in a [[Language (computability)|language]]. A certificate is often thought of as a solution path within a verification process, which is used to check whether a [[Decision problem|problem]] gives the answer "Yes" or "No". 

In the [[decision tree model]] of computation, certificate complexity is the minimum number of the <math>n</math> input variables of a [[decision tree]] that need to be assigned a value in order to definitely establish the value of the [[Boolean function]] <math>f</math>.

== Use in definitions ==

The notion of certificate is used to define [[semi-decidability]]:<ref>{{cite web|last=Cook|first=Stephen|title=Computability and Noncomputability|url=https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~sacook/csc463h/notes/comp.pdf|accessdate=7 February 2013}}</ref> a [[formal language]] <math>L</math> is semi-decidable if there is a two-place predicate [[Relation_(mathematics)|relation]] <math>R \subseteq \Sigma^* \times \Sigma^*</math> such that <math>R</math> is [[Computability|computable]], and such that for all <math>x \in \Sigma^*</math>:
    x ∈ L ⇔ there exists y such that R(x, y)

In this definition, y is the certificate, or witness, for the membership of x in L.

Certificates also give definitions for some complexity classes which can alternatively be characterised in terms of [[nondeterministic Turing machine]]s. A language <math>L</math> is in '''[[NP (complexity)|NP]]''' if and only if there exists a polynomial <math>p</math> and a [[polynomial-time]] bounded [[Turing machine]] <math>M</math> such that every word <math>x \in \Sigma^*</math> is in the language <math>L</math> precisely if there exists a certificate <math>c</math> of length at most <math>p(|x|)</math> such that <math>M</math> accepts the pair <math>(x, c)</math>.<ref>{{cite book |last1= Arora |first1= Sanjeev |last2= Barak |first2= Boaz |url= http://www.cs.princeton.edu/theory/complexity/ |title= Complexity Theory: A Modern Approach |publisher= Cambridge University Press |date= 2009 |isbn= 978-0-521-42426-4 |chapter=Definition 2.1}}</ref> The class '''[[co-NP]]''' has a similar definition, except that there are certificates for the words ''not'' in the language.

The class '''[[NL (complexity)|NL]]''' has a certificate definition: a problem in the language has a certificate of polynomial length, which can be verified by a deterministic logarithmic-space bounded Turing machine that can read each bit of the certificate once only.<ref>{{cite book |last1= Arora |first1= Sanjeev |last2= Barak |first2= Boaz |url= http://www.cs.princeton.edu/theory/complexity/ |title= Complexity Theory: A Modern Approach |publisher= Cambridge University Press |date= 2009 |isbn= 978-0-521-42426-4 |chapter=Definition 4.19}}</ref> Alternatively, the deterministic logarithmic-space Turing machine in the statement above can be replaced by a bounded-error probabilistic constant-space Turing machine that is allowed to use only a constant number of random bits.<ref>A. C. Cem Say, Abuzer Yakaryılmaz, "Finite state verifiers with constant randomness," ''Logical Methods in Computer Science'', Vol. 10(3:6)2014, pp. 1-17.</ref>

==Examples==
The problem of determining, for a given graph <math>G</math> and number <math>k</math>, if the graph contains an [[Independent set (graph theory)|independent set]] of size <math>k</math> is in '''NP'''. Given a pair <math>(G, k)</math> in the language, a certificate is a set of <math>k</math> vertices which are pairwise not adjacent (and hence are an independent set of size <math>k</math>).<ref>{{cite book |last1= Arora |first1= Sanjeev |last2= Barak |first2= Boaz |url= http://www.cs.princeton.edu/theory/complexity/ |title= Complexity Theory: A Modern Approach |publisher= Cambridge University Press |date= 2009 |isbn= 978-0-521-42426-4 |chapter=Example 2.2}}</ref>

A more general example, for the problem of determining if a given Turing machine accepts an input in a certain number of steps, is as follows:
  L = {<<M>, x, w> | does <M> accept x in |w| steps?}
  Show L ∈ NP.
  '''verifier:'''
    gets string c = <M>, x, w such that |c| <= P(|w|)
    check if c is an accepting computation of M on x with at most |w| steps
    |c| <= O(|w|<sup>3</sup>)
    if we have a computation of a TM with k steps the total size of the computation string is k<sup>2</sup>
    Thus, <<M>, x, w> ∈ L ⇔ there exists c <= a|w|<sup>3</sup> such that <<M>, x, w, c> ∈ V ∈ P
